A natural follow-up: can a single diagnostic predict not only \emph{how much} pruning a model tolerates, but also \emph{which} pruning strategy to use? Token importance CV provides exactly this dual prediction. Table~\ref{tab:scaling_law} compares L2 norm-based and random removal at $k{=}0.5$ across three models with measured CV.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{L2 norm vs.\ random removal at $k{=}0.5$. The gap $\Delta$(R$-$L2) scales monotonically with CV: low-CV models require random selection (uniform importance $\rightarrow$ L2 degenerates to spatial clustering), while high-CV models tolerate either strategy.}
\label{tab:scaling_law}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Model & CV & Tokens & L2 SR (\%) & Random SR (\%) & $\Delta$(R$-$L2) \\
\midrule
$\pi_0.5$ & 0.055 & 768 & 33.4 & \textbf{69.4} & $+$36.0 \\
X-VLA & 0.151 & 50 & 43.4$\pm$0.8 & \textbf{70.3}$\pm$0.9 & $+$26.9 \\
OpenVLA & 0.215 & 256 & 39.2 & 35.8 & $-$3.4 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The gap decreases monotonically as CV increases: $+$36.0\,pp ($\pi_0.5$, CV$\,{=}\,$0.055) $\rightarrow$ $+$26.9\,pp (X-VLA, CV$\,{=}\,$0.151) $\rightarrow$ $-$3.4\,pp (OpenVLA, CV$\,{=}\,$0.215). The mechanism is intuitive. When tokens have near-uniform L2 norms (low CV), the norm ranking captures spatial artifacts rather than genuine importance differences. L2 norm-based selection then clusters on correlated patches and loses spatial coverage, while random selection preserves the uniform distribution these models depend on. As CV rises, a genuine importance gradient emerges that L2 norm ranking can exploit; the random-vs-L2 advantage vanishes and eventually reverses.

CV therefore serves as a dual predictor. First, it predicts tolerance class: low CV signals uniform criticality (sensitive to method choice but potentially robust under the right strategy), moderate CV signals a threshold or graded response, and high CV signals extreme fragility (catastrophic cliff). Second, it predicts optimal strategy: models below CV $\approx 0.15$ should use coverage-preserving methods (random or spatially uniform selection), while models above this threshold can benefit from importance-based scoring.

At extreme compression ($k{=}0.3$), the interaction partially reverses for $\pi_0.5$: L2 norm achieves 51.0\% vs.\ random 36.4\% ($\Delta{=}-$14.6\,pp favoring L2). This suggests the optimal strategy also depends on the absolute token budget; when very few tokens remain, even spatially clustered high-norm tokens provide more signal than a sparse random sample. Full analysis of this interaction appears in Appendix~\ref{app:cv_strategy_interaction}.
